extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, astronomers, and advanced students of celestial mechanics reading Newton's Principia (historical Latin edition)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and interpret the propositions, problems, and theoretical claims in a Latin excerpt of Newton's Principia concerning planetary gravities, lunar motion, tides, and related computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative gravitational influences of Sun, Jupiter & Saturn (opening paragraphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative proportionalities of gravitational attractions among Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn, and their resulting perturbations on planetary motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives numeric ratios comparing gravities (examples: Saturn on Jupiter vs Saturn on Sun; compositions of accelerative gravities of Sun in Saturn, Jupiter in Saturn & Jupiter in Sun given as 16, 81 & {16×81×2360}÷25 ≈ 122342), concludes Saturn's perturbation on Jupiter is small (max ≈ 2′), Jupiter's perturbation on Saturn relatively larger; suggests placing Saturn's orbic umbilic at common center of gravity of Jupiter & Sun to remove most error. Use these ratios to estimate perturbation magnitudes; context: demonstrating relative smallness of outer planetary perturbations on inner ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIV. Theor. XIV. Orbium Aphelia & Nodi quiescunt.
rubrics_metrics.description: Aphelia and nodes of orbits are stationary (quiescunt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References Prop. XI and earlier results: aphelia rest, as do nodes if orbits are plane; mutual actions of planets and comets produce only negligibly small inequalities. Corol. 1: fixed stars likewise quiesce because they keep their aphelia and nodes. Corol. 2: no sensible parallax from annual motion; stellar forces produce no sensible effects in solar system due to immense distances. Use for treating long-term orbital reference positions as fixed to first approximation; small mutual perturbations may be ignored for many calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XV. Theor. XV. Invenire Orbium transversas diametros.
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure to find transverse diameters of orbits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that transverse diameters are taken in the sesquialteral ratio of periodic times (per Prop. XV Lib. I), then individually augmented in ratio of the sum of the masses of Sun and planet to the first mean proportional between that sum and the Sun (per Prop. LX. Lib. I). This is a prescription for computing orbit dimensions accounting for mass sums; references prior propositions for step-by-step calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVI. Prob. I. Invenire Orbium Excentricitates & Aphelia.
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: find orbital eccentricities and aphelia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement: problem is completed by reference to Prop. XVIII Lib. I. (no further computational detail in this excerpt). Use referenced proposition for explicit method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVII. Theor. XVI. Planetarum motus diurnos uniformes esse, & librationem Lunæ ex ipsius motu diurno oriri.
rubrics_metrics.description: Planets rotate uniformly about their axes; the Moon's libration arises from its diurnal rotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from Law I and earlier corollaries: a uniformly rotating moon presents the same face to a displaced umbilic and thus shows libration in longitude; libration in latitude arises from inclination of lunar axis to orbital plane. Phenomena confirm these conclusions. Use this as theoretical basis for explaining observed lunar librations (longitude and latitude) from rotational dynamics and axis inclination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVIII. Theor. XVII. Axes Planetarum dimetris quæ ad eosdem axes normaliter ducuntur minores esse.
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetary diameters measured along lines drawn normal to their rotation axes are shorter (i.e., planets are flattened by rotation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: a rotating planet of fluid material will have parts moving outward toward equator, increasing equatorial diameter and reducing polar axis; Jupiter's equatorial diameter > polar (supported by Cassini & Flamsteed). Similar reasoning for Earth: if Earth were not slightly higher at equator, seas would flow toward poles. This is a physical criterion linking rotation-induced centrifugal effects to oblateness; observation (e.g., Jupiter) corroborates. Use to infer oblateness from rotation rate and to predict fluid redistribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIX. Prob. II. Invenire proportionem axis Planetæ ad diametros eidem perpendiculares.
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: determine the ratio of a planet's axis to its diameters perpendicular to that axis (i.e., quantify flattening).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides multi-step computation from centrifugal force to gravity ratios: computes ratio of centrifugal force to gravity for Earth at equator as 1:290 4/5; derives relations between spheroid and sphere gravities, and obtains numerical estimate for Earth equatorial-to-polar diameter ~ 692:689 (so equatorial excess ≈ 17 Parisian miles, ≈ 85,200 feet). Discusses dependence on planetary rotation period, density distribution (possible central concentration increases flattening), application to Jupiter (different rotation yields different flattening), and effects on pendulum lengths & gravity at various latitudes. Guidance includes explicit numeric intermediate ratios and cautions that results assume uniform density; if density varies, outcomes change. Use full computational method here to estimate planetary oblateness and related gravity variations; compare with pendulum experiments for empirical verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XX. Prob. III. Invenire & inter se comparare pondera corporum in regionibus diversis.
rubrics_metrics.description: Find and compare weights of bodies at different regions (latitudes, depths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem: weights of equal bodies on canal legs are reciprocally proportional to the distances from Earth's center (reciprocal to radii). From prior calculations, increment of weight from equator to pole ≈ proportional to square of sine of doubled latitude. Gives numerical examples using latitudes (Paris, Goree, Cayenne) and computes pendulum length ratios: Paris pendulum length for one second ≈ 3 Paris feet + 17/24 digit parts; pendulums elsewhere exceed Paris length by small fractions (81/1000, 89/1000, 90/1000 of a digit). Observations by French experimenters differ slightly, implying Earth denser at center than uniform model assumed. Guidance: use pendulum observations to refine Earth density model; weight variation computations assume spherical geometry and may be adjusted for interior density gradients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXI. Theor. XVIII. Puncta Æquinoctialia regredi, & axem Terræ singulis revolutionibus nutando bis inclinari in Eclipticam & bis redire ad positionem priorem.
rubrics_metrics.description: Equinoctial points regress, and Earth's axis nutates so that in each revolution it inclines twice toward the ecliptic and twice returns to its previous position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from earlier corollaries; notes nutation is very small and hardly sensible. Use as statement that precession and small nutational oscillations of Earth's axis are predicted by the principles, but are minute in magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXII. Theor. XIX. Motus omnes Lunares, omnesque motuum inæqualitates ex allatis Principiis consequi.
rubrics_metrics.description: All lunar motions and inequalities follow from the supplied principles (i.e., gravitational theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues analogously that major planets carrying satellites behave like Moon–Earth system: satellites have umbilics, their motions are perturbed by the Sun producing inequalities like the Moon's. Lists qualitative behaviors: faster motion & larger area swept near Earth, orbit less curved in syzygies than quadratures (ignoring excentricity effects), apogee progresses and nodes regress with unequal rates, latitudes vary more in quadratures than syzygies, etc. Notes many of these inequalities are small and some observed astronomers deny or minimize nodal motions; comparison with observations (Flamsteed, Cassini) discussed. Use to justify deriving satellite irregularities from lunar theory and to set expectations for observational magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXIII. Prob. IV. Motus inæquales Satellitum Jovis & Saturni à motibus Lunaribus derivare.
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: derive unequal motions of Jupiter's and Saturn's satellites from the lunar-motion theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives proportional relations among mean motions of nodes and apsides of satellites vs lunar values, derived from ratios of orbital periods (composite ratios listed). Provides expected numerical secular motions (example: an external satellite's node advances ≈ 9°34' per century relative to Moon's nodal motion scaled). States amplitudes (Æquationes maxima) of satellites' node and apsidal inequalities are approximately those of lunar counterparts and that the Variation seen from Jupiter for the outer satellite does not exceed ~6″.22′ (small). Notes that smallness and slowness render satellite motions very regular and that recent astronomers sometimes deny nodal motion or call it very slow; observational comparisons (Flamsteed vs Cassini) mentioned. Use to compute predicted irregularities for planetary satellites using lunar analogues, with adjustment factors given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXIV. Theor. XX. Fluxum & refluxum Maris ab actionibus Solis ac Lunæ oriri debere.
rubrics_metrics.description: The flux and reflux (tides) of the sea arise from the actions of the Sun and Moon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive tidal theory: predicts two floods and two ebbs daily (in open sea), with maximum sea height occurring about the third lunar hour after the body's transit; solar and lunar effects combine (syzygy/ opposition produce maxima, quadratures minima). Lunar effect is larger than solar; times of high tide shift between syzygies and quadratures accordingly. Tidal force depends on distances (effects vary in the triplicate ratio of apparent diameters, i.e., inverse-cube dependence on distance), and also on declination (distance from equator) and latitude (leading to two hemispheric tidal waves opposed with 12 lunar-hour spacing). Gives examples and observational data: Plymouth/Bristol tide differences (≈ 1 foot to 15 digits), Tunquin/Batsham port with single daily tide due to basin/strait configuration, propagation through straits causing phase lags, and possibility of composed tides from different oceanic sources causing single rather than double daily tides. Also discusses persistence (inertia) of sea motion and modulation around syzygies/quadratures (third vs first/second tide). Guidance includes how to apply theory to local ports, expect delays/proportions, and to use local geometries and propagation through channels to explain deviations from open-sea predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXV. Prob. V. Invenire vires Solis ad perturbandos motus Lunæ.
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: find the forces from the Sun that perturb the Moon's motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets geometric construction (Q = Sun, S = Earth, P = Moon) and decomposes solar gravitational acceleration into components affecting lunar motion (QM reduced to QK, QL etc.), identifies parts QM and LM and their perturbative constituents SM and ML. Quantifies magnitudes: gives ML (mean solar perturbing force) relative to gravity at Earth's surface as 1:638092 (i.e., very small), using ratios of lunar and terrestrial periods and orbital distances. Guidance: shows how to decompose solar acceleration into components that perturb lunar orbit and gives numeric scale for perturbation relative to terrestrial gravity, useful for subsequent perturbation calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVI. Prob. VI. Invenire incrementum areæ quam Luna radio ad Terram ducto describit.
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the (hourly) increment of the area which the Moon's radius vector to Earth describes — i.e., determine how solar perturbation alters the area swept per equal times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assuming circular lunar orbit and neglecting other inequalities, derives the variation (increment) of hourly area swept due to solar perturbation. Uses approximations treating QP and QS as nearly parallel (Sun distant) and reduces varying forces to mean values; resolves perturbing force into radial and transverse components (SE and EL), shows EL (perpendicular) accelerates or retards area sweep. Produces numerical ratios: in octants the maximum EL exceeds ML by 3:2; computes that area momenta in syzygies vs quadratures are in ratio 11965:11865 under certain assumptions; when corrected for synodic period the ratio becomes 10973:11073 and general formulas are given. Final approximate expression: the area described in equal times ≈ sum of the number 219 46/100 and the sinus-versus (sinus versi) of twice the distance of the Moon from quadrature in a unit circle; notes modifications if the Variation is larger or smaller in octants. Guidance: gives concrete numeric factors (11915, 11965, 11865, 11023, 10973, 11073 etc.) and prescribes how to adjust for the synodic period; applicable for computing lunar area anomalies and thereby variations in angular motion and distance when observing hourly motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVII. Prob. VII. Ex motu horario Lunæ invenire ipsius distantiam à Terra.
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Moon's hourly (angular) motion infer its distance from Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States: the area swept by the moon about Earth in equal small time intervals is proportional to the product of the hourly motion and the square of the lunar distance; hence lunar distance is in the composite ratio formed by the square-root of area (direct) and the square-root inverse of the hourly motion. Corol.1: gives apparent lunar diameter (reciprocal to distance). Corol.2: allows more accurate construction of the lunar orbit from phenomena than before. Guidance: instructs astronomers to test this rule against observations to derive lunar distances and apparent diameters from measured hourly motions and area increments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVIII. Prob. VIII. Invenire diametros Orbis in quo Luna absque excentricitate moveri deberet.
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the diameters of the orbit in which the Moon would move if it had no eccentricity (i.e., construct an equivalent circular orbit accounting for perturbations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begins from curvature relations: curvature of trajectory (with perpendicular drawn) is proportional to attraction divided by square of velocity. Uses decomposed solar perturbations (attractio Lunæ in Terram as excess of lunar gravity over solar components) with expressions depending on AS and CS etc., leading to complex algebraic ratios for curvature in syzygies vs quadratures. Assumes ellipse DBCA (Earth at center S) with major axis DC at quadratures and minor AB at syzygies; constructs mapping of points on ellipse to a curve Cpa in a plane without angular motion to evaluate curvature relations, using ratios of synodic to periodic motions (29d12h44m vs 27d7h43m). Produces algebraic curvature relations (long expressions involving AS, CS, N, and numeric coefficients such as 120407, 122611, 2151969, 2191371, and 16824/100000) and prescribes how to compute the diameters of the hypothetical circular orbit without eccentricity via these curvature comparisons. Guidance: intended for theoretical computation of an equivalent circular orbit, using curvature and perturbation decomposition; requires long algebraic manipulation and prior definitions of the ellipse parameters.
